in_text_mentions: dry and broken areas of skin between the second, third, and fourth digits of both feet. The patient had been experiencing such pruritic lesions on both elbows, as well as portions of the proximal radial and ulnar regions, and the posterior knee areas for several years. During this presentation, the vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were normal. The skin examination revealed a draining malodorous lesion between the first and second digits, and dry, cracked areas between the second, third, and fourth digits of both feet (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single H&E biopsy image from plantar foot in Case 2 diagnosed as tinea pedis. Caption and in-text state hyperkeratosis with thickened stratum corneum and acanthosis; hyphae not readily visualized on H&E but case confirmed as tinea pedis by PAS in Figure 8. Histologic hyperkeratosis maps to moccasin-type plantar hyperkeratosis vocabulary term.
panels.attribution_text: Cohen et al. Tinea Corporis and Tinea Pedis Can Masquerade As Other Cutaneous Conditions in Decedents: Forensic Dermatology of Dermatophyte Infections.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.101452. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 7.
panels.figure_caption: Hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides of tinea pedis in Case 2. Microscopic examination of a biopsy from the plantar foot shows hyperkeratosis, with a thickened stratum corneum consisting of compact orthokeratosis (open black bracket). In contrast to acquired ichthyosis, the granular layer is present beneath the stratum corneum (between the black arrows). The epidermis beneath the stratum corneum is also thickened (acanthosis). Fungal hyphae in the stratum corneum (open black bracket) are not readily visualized on the hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections (hematoxylin and eosin stain, x20).
in_text_mentions: A biopsy of the plantar foot showed thickened stratum corneum (hyperkeratosis) and thickening of the epidermis (acanthosis). Dermatophyte hyphae could not be noticed on the hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections of the epidermis (Figure 7). However, the periodic acid-Schiff-stained sections clearly confirmed the presence of hyphae in the stratum corneum (Figure 8).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: PAS-stained human skin biopsy showing PAS-positive fungal elements at the stratum corneum–stratum lucidum junction; article is a case series of tinea pedis with atypical dermatophyte localization in the stratum lucidum (tinea lucidum variant). [raw subtype: tinea lucidum (stratum lucidum localization)] B: H&E-stained biopsy from the same tinea lucidum (tinea pedis variant) case showing eosinophils and lymphocytes; no matching vocabulary finding_key exists, so findings are listed as proposed. [raw subtype: tinea lucidum (stratum lucidum localization)]
panels.attribution_text: Gupta et al. Atypical Dermatophyte Localization in the Stratum Lucidum: A Retrospective Histopathologic Case Series of Tinea Pedis. Journal of fungi (Basel, Switzerland) 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic examination of tinea lucidum. (A) PAS staining showing florid fungal density along the stratum corneum–stratum lucidum junction and evidence of superficial perivascular inflammation. Light green arrows indicate fungal elements. (B) H&E staining showing the presence of eosinophils (yellow arrow) and lymphocytes (blue arrow). SC, stratum corneum; SL, stratum lucidum; SPV, superficial perivascular inflammatory infiltrate.
in_text_mentions: e present. The composition of inflammatory infiltrates was mostly chronic (e.g., lymphocytes, macrophages) in both acral and non-acral skin (Table S3). However, eosinophilic infiltrates were numerically more common in non-acral skin (11.5% [9/78] vs. 6.0% [9/149]; Z = 1.5, p = 0.15), although this difference was not statistically significant. Figure 3A illustrates a case of tinea lucidum with superficial perivascular inflammation and florid fungal densities at the stratum corneum–stratum lucidum junction and Figure 3B reveals the inflammatory composition containing eosinophils and lymphocytes.

However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as the possibility of selection bias cannot be excluded due to retrospective and convenience sampling. When examining dermatophyte distribution within the stratum corneum, a full thickness pattern was more frequently observed when dermatophyte invasion extended into the stratum lucidum (77.9% [53/68]), compared with cases in which dermatophytes were restricted to the stratum corneum alone (41.4% [53/128]; p < 0.0001). B: Higher-magnification PAS image of same acral plantar sample with fungal elements in stratum corneum. C: PAS histology of dorsal foot with dermatophytes in stratum corneum and lucidum; atypical localization in a tinea pedis case series. D: Higher-magnification PAS image of non-acral dorsal foot with fungi in stratum corneum and lucidum.

in_text_mentions: .2% [39/149]; p < 0.0001). However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as the possibility of selection bias cannot be excluded due to retrospective and convenience sampling. When examining dermatophyte distribution within the stratum corneum, a full thickness pattern was more frequently observed when dermatophyte invasion extended into the stratum lucidum (77.9% [53/68]), compared with cases in which dermatophytes were restricted to the stratum corneum alone (41.4% [53/128]; p < 0.0001). Examples of different dermatophyte localization patterns are shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

panels.figure_caption: A 79-year-old male patient (patient 4) whose punch-biopsy specimen obtained from the lateral foot (a non-acral site) showed dermatophyte localization (T. rubrum) restricted to the stratum lucidum (tinea lucidum). The patient had a history of chronic tinea pedis with persistent pruritus. (A–C) Xerosis, erythema, and papules are present on the dorsal, medial, and lateral aspects of the feet. (D,E) The infection progressed to secondary cellulitis. (F) Dystrophic toenail changes are present, consistent with onychomycosis, and (G) hyperkeratosis of the plantar aspect of the feet is present, consistent with moccasin-type tinea pedis.
